mean: a little angry about something that keeps bothering you
ex: Sameer was annoyed when the cable went off just before the last over.
ex2: The teacher looked annoyed as phones kept ringing during the parents' meeting.
note: Annoyed with a person, annoyed about or at a thing. It is milder than angry.

mean: impatient and slightly angry because something keeps bothering you
ex: Passengers grew irritated as the Mumbai local stood still for twenty minutes without any announcement.
ex2: Leela gets irritated when her brother hums the same film song while she is studying.
note: 'Irritating' describes the thing; 'irritated' describes how you feel. 'The noise is irritating; I am irritated.'

mean: unhappy and tired of something that has gone on too long
ex: The farmers were fed up with waiting three months for payment from the sugar mill.
ex2: Ritu is fed up with her old phone, which dies by lunchtime every day.
note: Say 'fed up with' in careful writing; 'fed up of' is common in speech but less formal.

mean: to disappoint someone who trusted you to do something
ex: Fans felt let down when their star skipped the final for an advertisement shoot.
ex2: Voters in the ward felt let down after the promised drains were never built.
note: The person goes in the middle: 'You let me down.' For the feeling, say 'I felt let down.'

mean: a statement that you are unhappy with something, often made officially
ex: Ayesha filed a complaint with the airline after her bag reached Chennai two days late.
ex2: The hostel warden received a complaint that the mess served the same dal every day.
note: Complaint against a person, complaint about a thing. 'Complain' is the verb, not the noun.

mean: sad because something was not as good as you hoped
ex: Kabir was disappointed with his marks, though he had studied every night for a month.
ex2: We were disappointed by the new restaurant in Koramangala: the biryani was cold and bland.
note: A calm 'I'm disappointed' often works better than shouting; it shows you expected better.

mean: too bad to be allowed or put up with
ex: The principal said that bullying juniors in the hostel was completely unacceptable.
ex2: Waiting six hours in a hospital corridor with a high fever is unacceptable, and Rehana told the manager so.
note: A firm but polite word for complaints: 'This delay is unacceptable' is stronger than 'This is very bad.'

mean: to suddenly become very angry and show it
ex: Try not to lose your temper with the call centre staff; they did not create the problem.
ex2: Coaches tell young players: never lose your temper with the umpire, however bad the decision.
note: Change 'your' to fit: 'He lost his temper.' 'Keep your temper' means stay calm.

mean: to let out anger or frustration by talking about it
ex: After a tough shift at the hospital, Neha calls her sister just to vent.
ex2: Many fans vent on social media after India loses, then calm down by morning.
note: 'I just need to vent' tells the listener you want them to listen, not to solve the problem.

mean: angry and hurt for a long time because you feel treated unfairly
ex: Chacha is still bitter that his younger brother got the ancestral house in Jaipur.
ex2: After losing the final on penalties, the players gave short, bitter answers to reporters.
note: Bitter anger is old and lasting, close to 'resentful'. It is also a taste: bitter gourd is karela.

mean: upset because someone said or did something rude or disrespectful
ex: Nani was offended when the guests left the wedding lunch without tasting her special kheer.
ex2: Joseph was offended by the joke about his accent, though his colleagues said it was harmless.
note: 'Don't be offended, but...' usually comes before something that may offend. The noun is 'offence' in British spelling.

mean: unhappy and annoyed, especially about how you are treated
ex: Disgruntled delivery workers in Hyderabad switched off their apps to protest the cut in pay per order.
ex2: A disgruntled shareholder stood up at the meeting and asked why profits kept falling.
note: Usually describes people with an ongoing complaint: disgruntled staff, customers or fans.

mean: feeling that you have been treated unfairly
ex: The aggrieved farmers said the compensation for their land was half the market rate.
ex2: Feeling aggrieved after being skipped for promotion, Meenakshi asked HR for a written explanation.
note: In law, the 'aggrieved party' is the person who was wronged. More formal than 'upset'.

mean: shocked and disgusted by something very bad
ex: Visitors were appalled by the garbage piled up beside the temple tank.
ex2: Doctors were appalled to find expired medicines being sold at the village chemist.
note: Stronger than 'shocked': it adds moral disgust. 'Appalling' describes the thing itself.

mean: very angry because something seems deeply wrong or unfair
ex: Parents were outraged when the school raised fees by forty percent in the middle of the year.
ex2: Cricket fans were outraged when tickets for the final cost more than a month's salary.
note: Outrage is anger at injustice, often shared by many people at once.

mean: to say that you do not agree with or do not like something
ex: Residents object to the plan to cut forty old trees for a parking lot.
ex2: Many students object to the new rule that the hostel gates close at eight.
note: Followed by a noun or -ing: 'I object to being shouted at', not 'I object to be shouted at'.

mean: to stay quietly angry for a long time, close to exploding
ex: Anger over the water shortage began to simmer in the colony long before anyone protested.
ex2: Through the long meeting, Faisal sat silent, letting his annoyance simmer as his idea was ignored.
note: 'Simmer down' means calm down. In the kitchen, dal simmers on low heat, just below boiling.

mean: to be very angry inside without fully showing it
ex: Kiran had to seethe in silence while the client blamed her team for his own mistake.
ex2: Fans began to seethe as the umpire ignored an obvious no-ball shown on the big screen.
note: Stronger than simmer. Often used as 'She was seething.' The 'th' is soft, as in 'breathe'.

mean: extremely angry
ex: Papa was livid when he found out the mechanic had charged ten thousand rupees for a fake repair.
ex2: The captain was livid after his batsmen threw away their wickets in the last five overs.
note: Informal and strong. It rhymes with 'vivid'.

mean: to keep causing bitter feelings long after something happened
ex: It still seems to rankle with Harpreet that the coach picked his own nephew for the state team.
ex2: The unfair fine from the society committee continued to rankle long after Mr Iyer had paid it.
note: The subject is the event, not the person: 'The remark rankled with him', not 'He rankled.'

mean: very angry, often loudly and openly
ex: An irate passenger shouted at the airline staff after his flight was cancelled for the third time.
ex2: Irate residents blocked the road in Patna after a week without electricity.
note: Common in news reports, as in 'irate customers'. More formal than 'furious'.

mean: annoying and unfair in a way that hurts your pride
ex: It was galling for Sanjana to see a copy of her project win the prize.
ex2: It is galling to pay toll every day for a highway full of potholes.
note: Usually in 'It is galling to...' or 'It is galling that...'. It is about unfairness that stings.

mean: extremely angry, usually at something unfair or insulting
ex: The weavers were incensed when a big brand copied their traditional designs without credit.
ex2: Ananya was incensed to learn the vegetable seller had been cheating her grandmother on the weight.
note: Formal and strong. Stress the second syllable, in-SENST, unlike incense sticks (IN-sens).

mean: a feeling of being offended, usually in the phrase 'take umbrage'
ex: The senior doctor took umbrage at the intern questioning his diagnosis in front of patients.
ex2: Some fans took umbrage at the commentator calling their state team 'minnows'.
note: Almost only used in 'take umbrage at'. It can sound slightly mocking, as if someone is easily offended.
